en: And forty blessings from Kydyr.
He became known as precious Bakai,
And received blessings from men of wisdom.
He taught the ignorant to know,
And set a thousand upon the right path.
My forefather, elder Bakai,
Before the magnanimous lion
Gathered ninety holy men,
And had them solemnly perform the marriage.
Elder Bakai the peacemaker,
After giving the poor daughter of Kaiypchal
In marriage to the bloodthirsty hero,
Like stars in the heavens
They stirred together,
And the two lions embraced,
Lioness and lion together;
Once they had united,
Like fine white-wheat flour
They blended into one,
Like the soft down of a white gazelle
They slipped together.
They sank into delight,
And lay upon one bed;
They settled in a fitting place,
And joined as husband and wife.
Because of a calamitous affair,
Sarybai, son of the ogre—
For all that Sarybai possessed,
Against that infidel son of the ogre
A swung sword could not cut,
A lion’s teeth could not pierce,
And human strength could not prevail.
Because of Sarybai’s wrath,
And the venom he poured upon the people,
Brave Semeñ, son of Manas,
Took Kuyaly, daughter of Kaiypchal,
The champion maiden, as his wife;
Then that champion maiden
Began the fierce combat.
The great epic is a mighty wonder;
Many times they fought.
Of savage infidel Sarybai,
She told the whole tale.
Kaiypchal and the Ogre
Shared the land where grain was sown,
Shared the people in splendid prosperity,
And shared the ground of fold and dwelling.
Speaking of humiliation and hardship,
Kuyaly, daughter of Kaiypchal,
Entered the great dispute.
Into a vast calamity with no end,
Into the turmoil she plunged.
She told of the ridge
Of a pass no mortal could cross.
Of the clash with Sarybai,
Of countless ordeals and great commotion,
She told the whole conflict.
Of the great quarrel with Sarybai,
She began the epic, revealing its secrets.
The vast ordeal, the deep conflict—
That wondrous, mighty epic,
She told it all.
When God granted her wish,
The desire and purpose she had sought,
When God freely granted it,
She drew the reins of fleet-footed Jeljetpes
And turned his head.
The one she would grapple with was Sarybai,
Such was the savage enemy.
Gentle in nature and broad of heart,
Such was the champion maiden’s way.
She turned the horse’s head,
And of all the saintly heroes—
Lion Bakai and Kanykei,
And heroes such as these—
She now asked their blessing.
“Toward sunrise with banners streaming
Lay the road I myself once rode.
That infidel son of the ogre
This hand has speared seven times.
He split lungs and severed heads,
Stirred strife and spilled blood;
He was an enemy bearing a blood feud.
Let me wage the battle freely;
For the common folk, for the people,
Against the savage foe Sarybai,
Let me clash in combat.
My lion father, khan Bakai,
My aged mother Kanykei,
If you give your blessing, let me receive it.
For the common folk, for the people,
Let me wage the conflict fiercely.
If true death reaches me, let me die;
If what Creator Allah has ordained
Falls upon my brow, let me face it.
For the common folk, for the people,
For the lost magnanimous lion,
For my lion brother-in-law Külchoro,
Above all, for you,
For the countless downcast host,
For the blue-maned boy Seytek,
Let me face the true decree;
If true death reaches me, let me die!
For all the heroes, for you,
Let me sooner behold
The true realm whence none return.
If I am granted days of honor and success,
Let me grapple with Sarybai, whom I hunt,
And spill his blood.
Against the enemy who brought my father calamity,
Let me strike without mercy.
From the enemy who oppresses us,
Let me avenge six generations of my fathers.
If I find the means, let me plunge the villain
Into grievous misery.
If the Creator does not will it,
Let me die at the infidel’s hands.
Infidel and Muslim alike—
How many people have been beset by war?
The one I shall grapple with is Sarybai;
Such is the infidel’s nature.
God knows who shall die;
God knows whether one will turn back
And return safely from the villain.
His calamities are many, his venom strong;
He lays flat whoever encounters him.
His strength is extraordinary,
And his heroism is manifold;
His venom is potent, his nature harsh—
Such is the grievous work
Of this blazing Sarybai.
Once my bloodthirsty, blue-maned father-in-law
Was slaughtering the Chinese
At the height of the massacre.
He trampled the whole universe
And cleaved through it.
When the mighty Zulfiqar
Was destined to come into being.
When he subdued the teeming enemy
And waged war against them.
From the desert of Medina,
From the shore of Jön Turbas,
From this side of Künümdük,
From the fortress of Jan-Baspas,
It appeared to him from the unseen.
There was no cawing crow,
No croaking raven in flight,
No serpent slithering away,
No wild ass frolicking there;
By many decrees it came to him.
“It is unique upon the earth,” they said;
By Allah’s favor it appeared,
And was found upon the empty steppe.
There a mortal marked for death was found;
For the blue-maned lion hero
It was found by Allah’s decree.
Laid upon grass, it set it aflame;
Those it struck died in an instant.
When drawn in the dark of night,
Its edge burned red with flame.
When swung against a formidable foe,
It lengthened to forty fathoms.
When drawn in wrath,
It never went without drinking blood.
Until it was fully sated with blood,
It would not return to its sheath.
My father-in-law’s Zulfiqar—
I desire to take it.
Against the infidel son of the ogre,
If I reach him, let me wield the sword.
Let me test myself in true combat,
And truly spill his blood.
The Zulfiqar inherited from our forefather—
If you give it, I shall gladly take it.
Against the infidel son of Sarybai,
I shall confront him and wage battle.
Seizing each other by the collar and dragging,
Struggling and hauling one another,
Striking with keen-edged swords,
Letting precious scarlet blood
Flow as we slash and crush—
Such a battle shall I wage.
If fate arrives and my days are done,
I shall surrender my dear life.
Does not every living mortal behold
The decree laid down by my Lord?
Does one not die when fate arrives?
Does a hero not die for honor?
Let me attempt the struggle;
If I do not die then, one day I shall.
For dignity and honor,
Let me join the fray.
To wage battle without restraint,
To ride out onto the field,
To brighten the hero’s brow,
To ease the ache of longing,
To issue the command,
To thrust and duel with spears,
To fight until all are spent,
To take a warrior’s life in hand,
To thrust the spear without tiring—
I learned from the transmitters,
And asked those who knew.
Its shaft is stout, its point is sharp,
With black steel fixed upon its tip;
Master of every craft,
A friend of the prophet David,
The forest smith fashioned it.
The base of the grain-dark spindlewood shaft
Was torn out with its roots.
At the fullness of summer,
Bull-necked and camel-thighed,
It destroyed men when they struggled.
The ill-omened, doom-bringing weapon
Was braced by champions.
They sheathed it in elephant hide
And thus began this great commotion.
“Summer days bring scorching heat,” they said,
“And when men grapple and fight,
It might suddenly break,” they said,
So they had it tempered in a shaded place.
“Those who take it will wage battle,” they said;
“When fierce combat and tumult arise,
The sword’s edge will strike,” they said,
So that no steel blade could cut it,
They bound it with white gold
And fashioned its many ridges.
When it came within reach
Of the holy man in your town,
When he cornered the one
Who had defied him,
He stretched and seasoned its shaft.
The patterned spear of your mighty champion—
Bölökbai and forty Kalmyks
Fashioned it with great distinction.
While they were making the spear,
A calf was slaughtered for the viewing,
And a whole forest was felled in the desert.
When the time came to temper it,
The black water boiled away to nothing.
When thrust bottomlessly at the foe,
Upon the head of whoever it struck,
Everything vanished in utter ruin.
They joined and fitted its point;
So that every one it struck
Might have his soul leave through his side,
They tempered it with tears.
Give me the splendid patterned spear,
The blue-flashing one, and let me take it;
Against the infidel son of the ogre
Let me clash and wage battle.
If true death reaches me, let me die;
Let me break the ribs
Of the enemy I truly fight.
Such is the manner of the struggle;
Let me take what I desire.
